title: The Gutter That Drank the Rain

pages.text: The rain came down so hard that the school yard turned brown. Zakari watched from the classroom door as water crept along the corridor and soaked his sandals. “Why is the water not going away?” he asked. Madam Boadi put on her raincoat. “Let us go and ask the water,” she said.
sentences: The rain came down so hard that the school yard turned brown.
Zakari watched from the classroom door as water crept along the corridor and soaked his sandals.
“Why is the water not going away?” he asked.
Madam Boadi put on her raincoat.
“Let us go and ask the water,” she said.
pages.alt: Heavy rain falls on a school yard while brown water spreads along a corridor and a boy stands in the doorway.

pages.text: Zakari, Korkor and Madam Boadi followed the gutter beside the school wall. The water was not rushing along it. It was standing still, like a pond. At one place it bubbled up and spilled over the edge. “Here is the problem,” said Korkor. “The gutter is full, but of the wrong thing.”
sentences: Zakari, Korkor and Madam Boadi followed the gutter beside the school wall.
The water was not rushing along it.
It was standing still, like a pond.
At one place it bubbled up and spilled over the edge.
“Here is the problem,” said Korkor.
“The gutter is full, but of the wrong thing.”
pages.alt: A concrete gutter overflowing with brown water beside a school wall, children and a teacher looking down.

pages.text: Madam Boadi poked the blockage with a long stick. Out came empty sachets, plastic bottles, a torn shoe and a thick layer of red mud. “Some of this is rubbish that people threw in,” she said. “And some is soil. When the ground is bare, rain washes the soil into the gutter. Mud blocks the flow first, and then the plastic gets caught in it.”

pages.alt: A teacher lifts sachets and a bottle on a long stick from a mud-filled gutter while children look on.

pages.text: “Does it matter if the water just sits there?” asked Zakari. “It matters a lot,” said Madam Boadi. “Still water is where mosquitoes lay their eggs, and mosquitoes can spread malaria. Water that cannot leave also floods yards, classrooms and homes. Gutters are meant to carry rain away, not to hold it.”
sentences: “Does it matter if the water just sits there?” asked Zakari.
“It matters a lot,” said Madam Boadi.
“Still water is where mosquitoes lay their eggs, and mosquitoes can spread malaria.
Water that cannot leave also floods yards, classrooms and homes.
Gutters are meant to carry rain away, not to hold it.”
pages.alt: A close picture of still brown water with mosquito larvae wriggling near a plastic sachet.

pages.text: They walked on, past houses and shops, until the gutter joined a bigger drain. The big drain ran towards a lagoon in the distance. “Every gutter is a small road for water,” said Korkor. “If one small road is blocked, the water has nowhere to go.” Madam Boadi smiled. “And every drain in a town joins others, so one blocked place can flood a whole street.”

The big drain ran towards a lagoon in the distance.

“And every drain in a town joins others, so one blocked place can flood a whole street.”
pages.alt: A map-like view of small gutters joining a big drain that flows toward a distant lagoon.

pages.text: Back at school, the headteacher brought two workers with a pickup and shovels. The children were not allowed to climb into the gutter, because that is dangerous. Instead they carried buckets, sorted the rubbish into bags and kept the compound clean around it. Soon the water began to move, slowly at first, then with a happy gurgle.
sentences: Back at school, the headteacher brought two workers with a pickup and shovels.
The children were not allowed to climb into the gutter, because that is dangerous.
Instead they carried buckets, sorted the rubbish into bags and kept the compound clean around it.
Soon the water began to move, slowly at first, then with a happy gurgle.
pages.alt: Workers shovel mud into a pickup while children sort rubbish into sacks at a safe distance.

pages.text: “But the gutter will block again,” said Zakari. “Yes, if we do nothing,” said Madam Boadi. “We must stop throwing rubbish in it. But we also need leaders to desilt drains, make them wide enough, cover the open ones and plant grass on bare ground. Children can do their part, and children can also ask grown-ups to do theirs.”
sentences: “But the gutter will block again,” said Zakari.

“We must stop throwing rubbish in it.
But we also need leaders to desilt drains, make them wide enough, cover the open ones and plant grass on bare ground.
Children can do their part, and children can also ask grown-ups to do theirs.”
pages.alt: Children write questions on a poster beside a clean gutter while a teacher points at a map.

pages.text: The next morning, the class made a poster: Bin it. Do not drain it. Korkor stuck it on the wall beside the gutter. Zakari counted the sachets in the school bin: forty-two before break time. “Last week they were in the gutter,” he said. “Today they are where they belong.” It was only a small change, but the water in the gutter ran clear. The end.
